10.1002_aenm.71332: Polymer electrolytes are key enabling materials for advanced energy‐storage and electro‐optical devices because they couple ion transport with interfacial stabilization, mechanical compliance, and operational safety within a single platform. While their roles in batteries and supercapacitors are well established, recent advances have extended their importance to multifunctional electrochromic systems, including electrochromic supercapacitors, electrochromic batteries, and smart windows, where electrochemical operation is directly coupled with reversible optical modulation. These systems impose tighter design constraints, requiring simultaneous control of ionic conductivity, electrochemical stability, optical transparency, switching uniformity, processability, and environmental durability. This review establishes the general design logic of polymer electrolytes in conventional energy‐storage devices by defining their core functions, major classes, and governing design variables. Representative systems are organized into hydrogels, organogels/ionogels, and free‐standing solid or semi‐solid electrolytes, highlighting how polymer chemistry, salt–solvent interactions, network architecture, and processing strategy govern device‐level behavior. This review discusses how these variables are reweighted in multifunctional electrochromic systems under coupled electrochemical and optical demands. By linking electrolyte classification with device‐dependent design criteria, this review provides a transferable framework for polymer‐electrolyte design across both conventional energy‐storage technologies and next‐generation electro‐optical systems.
10.1021_acs.analchem.6c02328: Flow imaging analysis (FIA), provides composition-agnostic morphological characterization. These measurements of particle size and shape are valuable to mass-based analysis, such as single particle inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (sp-ICP-TOFMS), which provides quantitative data on elements within particles. Using these two methods together enables informed use of geometric assumptions required by sp-ICP-TOFMS, as particle mass is typically converted to a particle diameter using assumed-spherical geometry. To validate this concept, parallel measurements to determine particle diameters were performed by FIA and sp-ICP-TOFMS on four particle suspensions: 300 nm polystyrene Eu-doped nanoparticles, 1 μm Fe-rich beads, 3 μm four element calibration polystyrene beads and 5 μm polystyrene beads. The Fe-particles obtained the highest percent difference from the manufacturer's nominal diameter, as the mean diameter obtained by FIA was overestimated by 21% and sp-ICP-TOFMS underestimated the mean diameter by 20.7%. Two types of particles were selected to test the effect of varying the particle number concentrations (PNC) on sizing accuracy, and both methods accurately sized each particle population at the PNC expected. Single particle analysis of carbon has continued to be a popular research topic, with direct applications to environmental pollutants in terms of nano- and micro- plastics. Real-world plastic particles were studied, and FIA's measured circularity values demonstrated that the particles deviated from spherical geometries, therefore sp-ICP-TOFMS data should be interpreted as mass-based rather than size-based. Combining these techniques enables improved interpretation of particle populations and evaluation of particle sizes.
